messages.author: ca76903a63dd0886
messages.subject: Extension of Stan manual example
parts:
Hi


I have a question on how one would extend an example in the Stan reference manual to additional crossed grouping structures.

I am referring to the multivariate normal example on page 144 of stan-reference-2.14.0. pdf. This example contains beta that vary by group J

model {

tau ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

Omega ~ lkj_corr(2);

to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0, 5); 

{

row_vector[K] u_gamma[J];

for (j in 1:J)

  u_gamma[j] = u[j] * gamma;

  beta ~ multi_normal(u_gamma, quad_form_diag(Omega, tau));

}

for (n in 1:N)

  y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * beta[jj[n]], sigma);

}

What would you suggest is the most efficient way to include an additional level that models variation from a crossed data structure, like with group M?

 

For example, intuitively I would think the varying coefficients should be specified with zero means, rather than the beta having mean u_gamma e.g.

parameters {

corr_matrix[K] Omega;

vector<lower=0>[K] tau;

vector[K] beta[J];

vector[K] alpha[M];

vector<lower=0> sigma;

vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_beta;

vector<lower=0>[M] sigma_alpha;

matrix[L, K] gamma;

} 

transformed parameters {

vector[N] gamma_hat;

for (n in 1:N)

  gamma_hat[n] = gamma + beta[jj[n]] + alpha[mm[n]]

}

model {

tau ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

Omega ~ lkj_corr(2);

to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0, 5);

for (j in 1:J)

  beta[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_beta);

for (m in 1:M)

  alpha[m] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

for (n in 1:N)

  y[n] ~ normal(x[n]*gamma_hat[n],sigma)

}

However, I then lose track of where one would specify the multivariate normal distribution of the overall model parameters, ~ multi_norm(gamma, quad_form_diag(Omega, tau)); as well as how to best specify beta and alpha. 


I have tried to run various tests, and from the results, I have the sense that I am on the wrong track. Any suggestions would be greaty appreciated!


Thanks

Andy

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Extension of Stan manual example
parts:
Usually that multivariate structure's just over the groups. Otherwise,
it would explode combinatorially and be very very hard to estimate.

The reason u_gamma looks the way it does is that there are predictors
for the group level parameters beta. If you convert into a non-centered
parameterization of beta, the u_gamma looks like an intercept and
the raw beta values get a prior with mean zero.

But you have to be careful when you introduce a bunch of groups with their
own intercepts because the model becomes non-identifiable except through the
priors.

- Bob
